metaData.originalTitle: 关于 AI 就业，1 亿条招聘数据背后的 5 个发现
metaData.title: 5 Findings on AI Employment from 100 Million Job Listings
metaData.oneSentenceSummary: Analysis of 100 million job listings reveals that while AI-related positions account for less than 2% of all jobs, the focus is shifting from building AI tools to using them. These roles command a salary premium of over 40% and show greater resilience, with the Chinese and US job markets diverging along different paths.
metaData.summary: Tencent Research Institute, in collaboration with the Institute of Population and Labor Economics at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, published the 'Big Data Research Report on New AI Career Trends.' Based on approximately 100 million public job listings from six major domestic recruitment platforms between Q1 2024 and Q2 2025, the report reveals five core findings. First, the penetration rate of AI-related jobs is about 1.6%-1.92%, on par with developed countries like the US, but the implicit penetration is deeper. The release of models like DeepSeek has acted as a catalyst for pulsed growth in job demand. Second, the growth in AI jobs is shifting from building tools to using them. The proportion of application-oriented roles has surged from less than 20% to 35% within a year. Among non-technical roles, AI penetration is growing fastest in consulting/analyst and design/creative categories. Third, unlike the US market where entry-level positions are shrinking, entry-level roles in China remain resilient due to differences in cost structures and industrial stages, though this may only be a temporary window. Fourth, AI jobs heavily favor highly educated and experienced professionals, with 71% requiring a bachelor's degree or higher and an average experience requirement 1.6-2.2 years above the market average. However, the signaling value of degrees is depreciating, with AI skills becoming an alternative credential. Fifth, the average salary premium for AI jobs remains above 40% and is more resilient, with high-salary ranges declining only half as much as the overall market during downturns. The report concludes that AI's impact on employment is not simply about job creation or destruction, but a rewriting of the logic of occupational stratification, requiring individuals, businesses, and education systems to adapt anew.

mainPoints.point: AI job penetration is less than 2%, but implicit penetration is deeper and accelerating in pulses.
mainPoints.explanation: Public job listings only count roles explicitly requiring AI skills, while many companies widely use AI tools in practice. The release of models like DeepSeek has acted as a catalyst for job demand, pushing the penetration rate back to 1.8% in Q1 2025.

mainPoints.point: Growth in AI jobs is shifting from building tools to using them, with application-oriented roles doubling in a year.
mainPoints.explanation: Application-oriented roles have surged from less than 20% to 35% of AI jobs. Among non-technical roles, AI penetration is growing fastest in consulting/analyst and design/creative categories, as companies urgently need talent to embed AI into business processes.

mainPoints.point: China's entry-level jobs have not seen the US-style shrinkage, but this resilience may only be a temporary window.
mainPoints.explanation: In the US, AI has led to a sustained shrinkage of entry-level jobs, while in China, these roles remain resilient due to lower labor costs and a different industrial stage. However, leaps in model capabilities and falling costs could rewrite this premise.

mainPoints.point: AI jobs command a salary premium of over 40% and are more resilient, but high pay does not guarantee safety.
mainPoints.explanation: The average monthly salary for AI jobs is 7,000-9,500 RMB higher than non-AI roles. During market downturns, high-salary ranges decline only half as much as the overall market. However, a distinction must be made between augmentation and automation roles, where high pay in the latter may be a buffer before obsolescence.

mainPoints.point: AI is rewriting the logic of occupational stratification, with degree signals depreciating and AI skills becoming an alternative credential.
mainPoints.explanation: AI jobs have extremely high educational requirements, but the share requiring a bachelor's degree has fallen from its peak. AI skills are replacing the signaling function of degrees, demonstrating learning ability and problem-solving skills, opening new paths for those without higher education.

keyQuotes: Although AI jobs are few, they are rewriting the rules on skill thresholds, hierarchical structures, and income ladders.

The US is using AI to replace entry-level employees; China is using AI to give entry-level employees a buff. But how long the buff lasts depends on the speed of model evolution and the curve of cost reduction.
High pay plus high replacement risk is the most dangerous combination: high pay makes you feel safe, while automation means you could be removed at any time.
What may be eliminated is not people, but abilities that cannot be amplified by AI and are easily replicated by it.
Mastering AI or staying away from AI could both be viable paths.

relatedArticles.title: After Large Models: Rewriting the Division of Labor Between Humans and Machines | A 10,000-Word Roundtable Transcript
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Through a roundtable dialogue between sci-fi writer Chen Qiufan and prompt engineering expert Li Jigang, this article deeply explores the reconstruction of human-machine division of labor in the era of large models: AI eliminates time barriers and takes over techniques, while humans must focus on ideas, taste, and intuition.

relatedArticles.title: The Era of Traffic 2.0
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article systematically discusses the paradigm shift of internet traffic from the 1.0 model centered on user attention to the 2.0 model centered on agent behavior and token consumption, and analyzes the profound impact of this transformation on various segments of the consumer internet and industry chain participants.

relatedArticles.title: When AI Makes Productivity No Longer the Bottleneck, What's Next? | AI Transition Survey 02 - flomo's Shaonan
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article features an in-depth conversation with Shaonan, co-founder of flomo, exploring the new bottlenecks teams face when AI contributes 70% of the code: lagging user value discovery, difficulties in restructuring collaboration, and how to redefine 'friction' and the value of note-taking in the AI era.

relatedArticles.title: Have We Just Celebrated Humanity's Last Labor Day? Eight Changes in AI's New Careers
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Based on an analysis of 1,570 job openings from seven AI-native companies on Labor Day 2026, this article reveals eight structural changes in the AI industry, including a doubling of total job postings, a shift in the workforce from R&D to commercialization, and an explosion in deployment roles, arguing that AI is accelerating the creation of new jobs even as it replaces others.

relatedArticles.title: Where is Education Headed in the Age of AI?
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article deeply explores the reconstruction of the underlying logic of education in the AI era, pointing out that the focus of education should shift from standardized knowledge transfer to cultivating core competencies that AI cannot replace, such as problem definition, cross-domain integration, and intrinsic motivation.

relatedArticles.title: Seven Questions on Tokenomics: An Introductory Map to the New AI Economy
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article systematically elaborates on the economic logic of Tokens as the core unit of measurement in the AI era, covering industrial background, value stratification, cost evolution, and future trends driven by autonomous agents.
